query: For multi-component concentrated alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their strength and deformation or failure behavior, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the conditions over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase multi-component concentrated alloys, deliberate composition changes that enhance short‐range order (SRO) and lattice distortion increase resistance to dislocation glide, resulting in higher yield strength and altered ductility compared to a baseline alloy with minimal SRO.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, equiatomic or near-equiatomic alloy system (e.g., a typical HEA) exhibiting minimal inherent SRO and lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by substituting or adding elements (for example, replacing a smaller element with one having a larger atomic radius) to promote increased atomic segregation and SRO (as seen in comparisons between alloys like CoCrFeNiPd versus CoCrFeNiMn).
generation.conditions: Tests performed under uniaxial tensile loading across a range of temperatures (e.g., from cryogenic to ~1073 K) and at controlled strain rates. In situ observations of dislocation dynamics (via TEM or neutron diffraction) should be conducted.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced degree of SRO and increased lattice distortions arising from the modified compositions.
generation.mechanism: The induced SRO and lattice distortions create local atomic scale barriers that disrupt the usual propagation of dislocations. These structural features require higher applied stress to enable dislocation motion, thereby increasing the yield strength and potentially modifying ductility (depending on temperature and strain rate).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy with enhanced SRO should exhibit a higher yield strength and a higher resistance to dislocation glide (evidenced by lower dislocation velocities and more rugged dislocation lines during in situ tests). At lower temperatures, these effects may be more pronounced, while at high temperatures diffusion-mediated processes may reduce the differences.
generation.baseline: A compositionally similar single-phase alloy designed to exhibit minimal SRO and lower lattice distortions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold in single-phase concentrated alloys (HEAs or RHEAs) where composition modifications do not induce secondary phases. Its applicability might be limited to systems where deformation is primarily controlled by dislocation glide rather than diffusional creep.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the yield strength increase and the ductility change is material-specific and may vary with temperature and strain rate. Additionally, interplay with other deformation mechanisms at very high temperatures introduces further uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys that are identical in processing history: one with baseline composition and another with a modified composition designed to enhance SRO and lattice distortion (by, for example, substituting elements to increase atomic size mismatch). Perform uniaxial tensile tests and in situ dislocation imaging (using TEM or neutron diffraction) at a range of temperatures and constant strain rates.
measurements: Yield strength and stress–strain curves to quantify mechanical strength
In situ observations of dislocation morphology and glide velocity
Characterization of SRO levels using atom probe tomography, X-ray diffraction or other appropriate techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in yield strength or exhibits similar dislocation dynamics (i.e., similar velocity profiles and dislocation morphologies) as the baseline alloy under the same testing conditions, the hypothesis that enhanced SRO and lattice distortions govern the observed mechanical strengthening will be falsified.

Theoretically, with the increase in the temperature, the dislocation movement becomes easier due to the decrease in the resistance to the dislocation movement and the increase in the dislocation movement mode, and the elongation at the fracture of the single-phase alloys increases [,,]. However, in this study, a low-plasticity plateau appeared when the temperature was between 873 K and 1073 K. In other words, in that temperature range, the alloy became more brittle compared to that at room temperature. Figure 6 shows the fracture diagram of the sample after tensile testing at 673, 873, and 1073 K. The specimens exhibited a ductile fracture at all three temperatures, and obvious dimples and fluvial patterns were observed from the fracture surface []. It is obvious from the figure that there is little difference between the fractures at all three temperatures. In addition, obvious black spots can be seen in all three images, which is the residue of the alloy oxidation. These oxides also show that the alloy was slightly oxidized during the tensile tests at high temperature.

In addition to twinning activities and GPFE curves, we further investigated the dislocation morphology and mobility at a constant strain rate or shear stress, with results indicating that there was a higher barrier for achieving equivalent dislocation velocity in HEAs than in Ni (Supplementary Fig. 9). The extended dislocation in HEA exhibited rugged dislocation lines and a significantly varied dissociation width, which differed markedly from that in Ni with smooth straight dislocation lines and a uniform SF width. Dislocation glide in the HEA was enabled via a series of forward slips by local segments after depinning from local heterogeneities,, and this resulted in nontrivial fluctuations in shear stress under a constant strain rate or in dislocation velocity under constant shear stress. Recently, Ding et al. synthesized FCC CoCrFeNiPd and CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. The former exhibited a higher yield strength than the latter with comparable tensile ductility. They proposed that the essential difference between these two HEAs was associated with atomic segregation and short-range ordering (SRO); both were enhanced in CoCrFeNiPd, as compared with CoCrFeNiMn. The idea was that SRO tends to create resistance to deformation/slip, leading to larger dislocation glide resistance in the more ordered CoCrFeNiPd than in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. Theoretical work by Yin et al. suggested that the strengthening was due mainly to the large atomic/misfit volume of Pd in CoCrFeNi. Ma et al. identified a number of unusual features associated with dislocations/slips in HEAs that were related to lattice distortion and/or local chemical order. SRO also occurs in medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). The atomic structure of a CoCrNi MEA indicates that Cr favors Ni and Co neighbors, reducing the electrical and thermal conductivities and increasing the stacking-fault energies and hardness.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) [] have gained much attention recently due to their unique solid solution hardening combined with high ultimate tensile strengths, uniform elongation, high cryogenic fracture toughness, and excellent ductility if consisting of a single phase face-centered cubic (fcc) with a large number of slip systems [,,]. CoNiCrFeMn alloy is such an equiatomic HEA with a single phase fcc structure firstly reported by Cantor et al. []. Although, the elements in this alloy possess different crystal structures, it crystallizes as a solid solution of single phase fcc. There are numerous experimental [,,,,,] and simulation [,,,] studies reporting the mechanical properties of CoNiCrFeMn alloy. Otto et al. [] reported an increment in the yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation to fracture with decreasing temperature especially in the cryogenic range. Surprisingly, ductility was also improved significantly at low temperatures with strength. Similar behavior was observed in the studies of Gludovatz et al. []. reading.lever: Modify alloy compositions to induce varying degrees of SRO and lattice distortion, then correlate dislocation mobility changes via in situ tests.
reading.why: Prior studies show that atomic segregation and lattice distortions from composition changes significantly alter dislocation behavior, providing a mechanistic handle on strength and failure in HEAs.
